text: in the back of the elementary school. It was where the severely disabled children were placed—kids with profound developmental disabilities, kids who would never read at all. I understood, even then, what that placement meant. I was broken in a way that couldn’t be fixed. It felt like I was being stored. But then she appeared. She was young—a recent graduate student who had just completed her master’s thesis on a condition that was only just beginning to be understood, called dyslexia. She heard about a boy who had been pulled from regular classes, a boy who seemed intelligent but couldn’t decode written language, and she asked if she could work with me. I don’t remember her face clearly. I don’t remember her name at all—I’ve searched for her to no avail. What I remember is an index card. She took a plain white index card and cut a small rectangle out of the center, just large enough to frame a single word. Then she handed it to me. “Slide this across the sentence,” she said. “But don’t move on until the word in the box makes sense.” That was it. That was her algorithm. She explained that my brain was seeing multiple possibilities for each word—letters rearranging into different configurations—and I was getting lost in the noise. But if I waited, if I held the word in that small window and considered the context of the word before it, my brain would eventually select the interpretation that fit. She told me that sometimes the next word might cause me to look back and adjust what the previous word was. She said to take it one word at a time and wait for meaning. That the right word would emerge. She said it would help rewire my brain. I didn’t understand what she meant at the time. I was ten years old. But I trusted her, and I did what she asked. Word by word. Sentence by sentence. Waiting for meaning to emerge from chaos. And it worked. Within months, I was reading. Not quickly, but still reading. The letters still moved sometimes, but I had learned to wait them out, to let context be my anchor. My brain, it turned out, could learn a new way to learn. Later that same school year—the year I had been placed with children who would never read—my teacher mentioned a statewide writing competition. The topic was “Why I Am Proud to Be an American.” We were studying the Constitution. I was practicing reading by rereading that amazing document over and over because rereading content I knew turned out to be very helpful in developing faster reading skills. I felt I might have something to say. Maybe I wanted to prove something to myself. Maybe I wanted to prove something to whoever had put me in that back room. I wrote my essay slowly and thoughtfully. Weeks later, the entire school was called to assembly. I was painfully shy and positioned myself at the back of the room, as far from attention as I could get. The principal announced that our school had produced a winner in the statewide competition. Third place went to a student from Houston. Second place went to a student from Austin. And I still remember like it was yesterday, the principal saying, “And the first-place winner is from Dallas, from our very own Skyview Elementary, Bobby Jay Keele.” Me! (I would later be adopted and change my name to Bob Burgin.) I stood in the back of that room in Dallas in disbelief, frozen, as my name echoed off the walls. The boy who, less than one year before, couldn’t read had submitted the best essay in the entire state of Texas. I didn’t even know how to respond. I remember looking over at the teacher who had rewired my brain. She was so very proud, I hope as much for herself as for me. *** I’ve thought about that teacher many times over the past fifty years—especially in the last fifteen, as I’ve devoted my career to understanding how humans learn and how that understanding might translate to machines that learn. When people say that AI is just predicting the right next word, I have a particular response to how that relates to intelligence. I have a deep sense of how predicting the next word based on associated meaning, and looking both backward and forward for context, creates intelligence. Something that I learned from an index card with my twenty-watt brain. What that teacher gave me wasn’t just a reading technique. She gave me a learning algorithm. She didn’t teach me what the words meant; she taught me how to learn to read with dyslexia. She created the conditions for my brain to rewire itself, to find signal in noise, to let meaning emerge from chaos. In chapter 1 of this book, I described how DeepMind’s AlphaGo defeated the world champion at Go—not because programmers taught it strategy, but because they taught it to learn. “We didn’t teach AlphaGo how to play Go,” I wrote. “We simply gave it the rules and let it play millions of games against itself. We taught it to learn—and it did.” That young teacher did the same thing with my ten-year-old brain. She gave me the rules—wait for context, let meaning resolve—and let my neural networks do the rest. She created the conditions for emergence. The title of this book is Emergence : the phenomenon by which complex behaviors arise not from any single part, but from the interactions among parts. When energy flows through a system in just the right way, patterns appear. Structure takes shape. Something novel emerges. I was that system. A twenty-watt brain, wired in a way that made reading nearly impossible, but capable—with the right algorithm—of rewiring itself. Of finding new pathways.
